entry: City on the Atlantic coast of northeastern [[Florida]] (pop., 2020: 949,611). It is the county seat of Duval County, with which it consolidated in 1968, and the largest city in the Southeast. The city covers 900 square miles (2,300 square kilometers) and straddles the St. Johns River. A platted town named for [[Andrew Jackson]] was established in 1822, a year after Spain ceded Florida to the United States. Harbor improvements since the late 19th century made Jacksonville a major [[Port|port]], home to the Port of Jacksonville and several military installations. Banking, insurance, healthcare, logistics and golf-related tourism are important to the economy.

Third Hebrew patriarch in Judaism, son of [[Isaac]] and Rebecca, later given the name Israel and an important figure in the Abrahamic religions. He first appears in the [[Torah]], where the [[Book of Genesis]] describes him as the twin brother of Esau. He is said to have bought Esau's birthright and, with his mother's help, deceived his aging father into giving him the blessing meant for Esau. After a severe drought in [[Canaan]], Jacob and his descendants migrated to [[Egypt]], where his son [[Joseph (Genesis)|Joseph]] had become a confidant of the pharaoh. Jacob is said to have died there at 147 and been buried in the Cave of Machpelah in [[Hebron]]. He had twelve sons and a daughter, Dinah, and his sons' descendants were collectively known as the [[Israelites]]. Mainstream archaeologists agree that no existing or recoverable evidence establishes Jacob as a historical figure.

Swiss mathematician and early proponent of Leibnizian [[Calculus|calculus]], to which he made numerous contributions. Born in [[Basel]], he studied theology at his father's wish but also pursued mathematics and astronomy. From 1676 to 1682 he traveled through Europe, learning the work of leading figures including Robert Boyle and Robert Hooke. He began teaching mechanics at the University of Basel in 1683 and was appointed professor of mathematics there in 1687, a post he held for the rest of his life. With his brother [[Johann Bernoulli|Johann]], he was one of the founders of the [[Calculus of variations]], and he discovered the fundamental mathematical constant [[E (mathematical constant)|e]]. His most important contribution was in [[Probability|probability]]: his work *Ars Conjectandi* contains the first version of the [[Law of large numbers]]. He sided with [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]] in the Leibniz–Newton calculus controversy.

[[Matrix (mathematics)|Matrix]] of all first-order [[Partial derivative|partial derivatives]] of a vector-valued [[Function (mathematics)|function]] of several variables, named after [[Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi]]. When the matrix is square, its [[Determinant|determinant]] is called the Jacobian determinant. The Jacobian matrix is the natural generalization of the [[Derivative|derivative]] to such functions and represents the best linear approximation of a function near a point. A differentiable inverse exists near a point exactly when the Jacobian determinant is nonzero there, and the determinant is used for changes of variables in [[Multiple integral|multiple integrals]].

Political movement, active from 1688 to the end of the 18th century, that sought to restore the exiled House of Stuart to the British throne. It was strongest in Ireland and the western [[Scottish Highlands]]. Jacobites argued that because kings held office by divine right, the regime installed by the [[Glorious Revolution]] of 1688 was illegitimate. Serious revolts came in 1715, 1719 and 1745, and French invasion attempts in 1708 and 1744. The 1745 Rising briefly threatened the Hanoverian monarchy, but its defeat in 1746 ended Jacobitism as a serious political movement.

Dutch Reformed minister and theologian whose views became the basis of [[Arminianism]] and the Dutch Remonstrant movement. He was orphaned young and adopted by a priest inclined toward [[Protestantism|Protestantism]]; he studied at Leiden from 1576 to 1582, then at Basel and Geneva, where he studied under Theodore Beza. He served from 1603 as professor of theology at the University of Leiden and wrote many books and treatises on theology. His challenge to the Reformed standard, the Belgic Confession, provoked discussion at the Synod of Dort, which drew up the five points of Calvinism in response to his teaching.

Dutch physical chemist and first recipient of the [[Nobel Prize|Nobel Prize in Chemistry]], in 1901, for discovering the laws of chemical dynamics and osmotic pressure in solutions. In 1874 he formulated the theory of the [[Tetrahedron|tetrahedral]] [[Carbon|carbon]] atom, now regarded as the foundation of stereochemistry. The theory was largely ignored at first and sharply criticized by Hermann Kolbe, but support from Johannes Wislicenus and Viktor Meyer brought recognition by about 1880. His work also helped found the modern theory of chemical affinity, [[Chemical equilibrium]], [[Chemical kinetics]] and [[Thermodynamics]]. In 1887 he co-founded, with [[Svante Arrhenius]] and Wilhelm Ostwald, the *Zeitschrift für physikalische Chemie*, the first dedicated journal of [[Physical chemistry]].

First Lady of the United States from 1961 to 1963, as wife of [[John F. Kennedy]]. She redefined the largely ceremonial role by hosting arts and cultural events at the [[White House]] and led its restoration as a historical site. Her style, known as the "Jackie Look", inspired fashion trends in the 1960s, and her cultural literacy improved the image of the United States during the [[Cold War]]. She was named [[Time (magazine)|Time]] magazine's Woman of the Year in 1962. In 1968 she married Greek shipping magnate [[Aristotle Onassis]], a union that drew controversy. After his death in 1975 she worked as a book editor in New York City, first at Viking Press and then at Doubleday. She is buried at Arlington National Cemetery beside President Kennedy.

French maritime explorer from [[Brittany]], the first European to describe and map the [[Gulf of St. Lawrence|Gulf of Saint Lawrence]] and the shores of the [[St. Lawrence River|Saint Lawrence River]]. In 1534, under a commission from King Francis I, he explored [[Newfoundland (island)|Newfoundland]], the Strait of Belle Isle, the Gaspé coast and [[Prince Edward Island]], where his crew killed around 1000 birds, most of them [[Great auk|great auks]]. On his second voyage (1535–1536) he sailed up the river to Stadacona, now [[Quebec City]], and Hochelaga, now Montreal, and wintered amid [[Scurvy|scurvy]] outbreaks. He named the region Canada after the Iroquoian names for those settlements. His third voyage (1541–1542) attempted a colony at Cap-Rouge that failed, and he never found a route to Asia or the precious metals he sought.

French naval officer, oceanographer, filmmaker and author. In 1943 he co-invented the Aqua-Lung with Émile Gagnan, the first successful open-circuit self-contained underwater breathing apparatus (SCUBA). His book *The Silent World* surmised the echolocation abilities of [[Porpoise|porpoises]]; the film adaptation, co-directed with Louis Malle, was one of the first to document the ocean depths in color. It won the Palme d'Or at the [[Cannes Film Festival]] in 1956 and an Academy Award for Best Documentary in 1957. From 1966 to 1976 he hosted the television series *The Undersea World of Jacques Cousteau*. In 1973 he founded the Cousteau Society to promote ocean conservation.

Algerian-born French philosopher who developed the philosophy of deconstruction. He developed it through close readings of [[Ferdinand de Saussure]]'s linguistics and of Husserlian and Heideggerian [[Phenomenology (philosophy)|phenomenology]]. Though he distanced himself from post-structuralism and disavowed the word postmodernity, he is one of the major figures associated with it. Derrida published over 40 books and hundreds of essays, and his influence reached [[Literature|literature]], law, [[Anthropology|anthropology]], historiography, [[Psychoanalysis|psychoanalysis]] and architecture. Critics, including [[Noam Chomsky]], contended that deconstruction undermines causal reasoning and empirical accountability. For the last two decades of his life he was professor in humanities at the University of California, Irvine.

French painter in the [[Neoclassicism|Neoclassical]] style, considered the preeminent painter of his era. In the 1780s his history paintings marked a shift in taste away from [[Rococo]] frivolity toward classical austerity and heightened feeling. He became an active supporter of the [[French Revolution]] and a friend of [[Maximilien Robespierre]], and was effectively a dictator of the arts under the French Republic. After Robespierre's fall he was imprisoned, then served [[Napoleon]] and developed the warm Venetian colors of the Empire style. After Napoleon's fall he exiled himself to [[Brussels]], where he remained until his death. His pupils made him the strongest influence on early 19th-century French art, especially academic Salon painting. His works include *The Death of Marat*, *Napoleon Crossing the Alps* and *The Coronation of Napoleon*.

Umbrella term for two decorative rocks, nephrite and jadeite, used for jewelry and ornaments. Nephrite, a [[Calcium|calcium]] and [[Magnesium|magnesium]] silicate of the amphibole group, is typically green but may be yellow, white or black. Jadeite, a [[Sodium|sodium]] and aluminum silicate of the [[Pyroxene|pyroxene]] group, ranges from near-colorless to green, including the emerald-green "imperial" variety, and also occurs in lavender, yellow, orange, brown and black. The English word derives from the Spanish *piedra de ijada*, or "flank stone", from its reputed use in curing ailments of the loins and [[Kidney|kidneys]]. Jade is especially prized in [[East Asia]], where Type A jade, natural untreated jadeite, is revered for purity and harmony.

Deity in [[Chinese folk religion]] and myth, also called Yudi or Heavenly Grandfather. In Taoist theology he is an assistant to Yuanshi Tianzun, one of the Three Pure Ones, the primordial emanations of the [[Tao]]. He is often identified with Śakra in Chinese Buddhist cosmology and with [[Yu the Great]] in Chinese mythology. In one myth he becomes monarch of all the deities in heaven after a war against a powerful evil entity. He is said to have allocated the [[Chinese zodiac]] through legendary races. His birthday festival, on the ninth day of the first lunar month, draws crowds to [[Temple|temples]], especially in Taiwan and southern [[China]].

Large cat species, *Panthera onca*, the only living member of the genus [[Panthera]] native to the Americas. It is the biggest cat in the Americas and the third-largest in the world, with a body length of up to 1.85 m (6 ft 1 in) and a weight of up to 158 kg (348 lb). Its powerful bite pierces the shells of turtles and tortoises, and it kills mammalian prey by biting through the skull between the ears. Its range runs from the southwestern United States through Mexico and [[Central America]] to the [[Amazon rainforest]], south to Paraguay and northern Argentina. An adept swimmer and solitary [[Apex predator]], it is a keystone species, and it is listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List because of habitat loss and killings by ranchers.

Basque sport of bouncing a ball against walls with a wicker basket glove called a xistera. It is a variation of Basque pelota, and the term, coined by Serafin Baroja in 1875, means "joyful party" in Basque. The sport is played worldwide, especially in [[Spain]], [[France]], the American state of [[Florida]] and the Mexican state of [[Baja California]]. Play takes place on a court with walls on three sides, and the first team to score 7 points (or 9 in Superfecta games) wins.

Capital and largest city of the northwestern Indian state of [[Rajasthan]] (pop., 2011: 3.1 million). Founded in 1727 by Sawai Jai Singh II, the Kachhwaha Rajput ruler of Amer, it is one of the earliest planned cities of modern [[India]], designed under the architectural guidance of Vidyadhar Bhattacharya. It was painted pink in 1876 to welcome the Prince of Wales, giving it the nickname Pink City. It became capital of the newly formed state of Rajasthan in 1949. The city forms part of the Golden Triangle tourist circuit with [[Agra]] and Delhi, and lies 268 km (167 mi) from [[New Delhi]]. Its historic center was inscribed on the [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage List]] in 2019, and Nobel laureate [[C. V. Raman]] called it the "Island of Glory".

Brazilian politician and former army officer, 38th president of Brazil from 2019 to 2023. He represented [[Rio de Janeiro (state)|Rio de Janeiro]] in the Chamber of Deputies from 1991 to 2019. He lost the 2022 election to [[Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva]]. On 8 January 2023, supporters stormed federal government buildings, calling for a [[Coup d'état|coup]]. In 2025 he was convicted of coup plotting and sentenced to 27 years and 3 months in prison; he denies the charges. Commentators describe his politics as far-right and populist, while supporters credit his pension reform and privatizations. His COVID-19 response drew significant criticism.

American actor, born in [[Los Angeles]]. He began acting as a child in *City Slickers* (1991) and had his breakthrough as Homer Hickam in *October Sky* (1999). He won a BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Supporting Role and received an Academy Award nomination for *Brokeback Mountain* (2005), directed by [[Ang Lee]]. His later films include *Zodiac* (2007), *Prisoners* (2013) and *Nightcrawler* (2014). He also starred in the Apple TV series *Presumed Innocent* (2024) and has performed on Broadway.

German merchant, mining entrepreneur and banker, known as Jakob Fugger the Rich. He expanded his family's textile business, built on trade with Italy, into a firm operating across Europe. The company began banking transactions with the [[House of Habsburg]] and the Roman Curia, and from 1493 extracted silver and [[Copper|copper]] in Bohemia and Hungary. By 1525 it also held the right to mine [[Mercury (element)|quicksilver]] and [[Cinnabar]] in Almadén. Fugger contributed to the election of Charles I of Spain as Holy Roman Emperor Charles V and helped finance the rise of Maximilian I. He founded the Fuggerei in Augsburg in 1521, the world's oldest social housing complex still in use. Journalist Greg Steinmetz estimated his wealth at around 2% of Europe's GDP at the time.

Medium-sized [[Chili pepper|chili pepper]] cultivar of *Capsicum annuum*, commonly picked while green and sometimes allowed to ripen to red, orange or yellow. Its pungency is usually between 4,000 and 8,500 units on the Scoville scale, and it is wider and generally milder than the similar serrano pepper. The name is Spanish for "from Xalapa", though the pepper is not grown in or around Xalapa; Vicente Jiménez invented the pickling and canning process there. Jalapeños were in use by the [[Aztecs]] before the Spanish conquest, when Aztec markets sold smoked jalapeños, called chipotles.

Killing of unarmed Indian civilians by British Indian Army troops in [[Amritsar]], Punjab, on 13 April 1919. Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer ordered troops to fire on a crowd in the Jallianwala Bagh, a garden with a single exit, which he blocked with his troops. Estimates of the dead range from 379 to 1,500 or more, with over 1,200 injured. [[Winston Churchill]] condemned it as "unutterably monstrous", and the House of Commons voted 247 to 37 against Dyer in 1920. The anger it provoked fed the non-cooperation movement of 1920–22. Britain has never formally apologized, though it expressed deep "regret" in 2019.

Island country in the [[Caribbean]], the third-largest island in the [[Greater Antilles]], with 2.8 million people. It covers 10,991 square kilometers (4,244 sq mi), and Kingston is the capital and largest city. After [[Christopher Columbus]] arrived in 1494, Spain ruled the island until England conquered it in 1655 and named it Jamaica. Under British rule it became a leading [[Sugar|sugar]] exporter with a plantation economy dependent on imported African slaves, and Britain emancipated all slaves in 1838. Jamaica achieved independence from the [[United Kingdom]] on 6 August 1962. It is a parliamentary [[Constitutional monarchy|constitutional monarchy]] and a Commonwealth realm with Charles III as king, and Andrew Holness has been prime minister since March 2016. The island is the birthplace of [[Rastafari]] and [[Reggae|reggae]], and tourism is central to its economy.

Saudi journalist, dissident and editor, assassinated at the Saudi consulate in [[Istanbul]] on 2 October 2018. Born in [[Medina]], he edited the Saudi newspaper *Al Watan*, seen as a platform for Saudi progressives. He fled Saudi Arabia in 2017, and in exile wrote critical articles about the government and Crown Prince [[Mohammed bin Salman]]. He entered the consulate to obtain documents for his marriage and was never seen leaving. The [[Central Intelligence Agency]] concluded that bin Salman ordered the killing. Saudi courts convicted lower-level operatives but denied high-level culpability.

American writer and civil rights activist, known for essays, novels, plays and poems. His 1953 novel *Go Tell It on the Mountain* was ranked by [[Time (magazine)|Time]] among the top 100 English-language novels. *Notes of a Native Son* (1955) established him as a voice for human equality. He moved to [[Paris]] in 1948 to escape racial hostility in the United States. [[Homosexuality|Gay]] and [[Bisexuality|bisexual]] men feature prominently in his fiction, as in *Giovanni's Room* (1956), and his work influenced both the [[Civil rights movement]] and the gay liberation movement. His 1965 debate with William F. Buckley is regarded as one of the most influential debates.
